assignments.text:
I never shall forget the dismay felt when a certain Captain
Brown came to live at Cranford, and openly spoke about his being poor—not
in a whisper to an intimate friend, the doors and windows being previously
closed, but in the public street! in a loud military voice! alleging his
poverty as a reason for not taking a particular house. The ladies of Cranford
were already rather moaning over the invasion of their territories by a man and
a gentleman.
assignments.summary: Captain Brown arrives in Cranford and scandalises the ladies by speaking loudly and openly about his poverty in the street.
assignments.best_quote: he openly spoke about his being poor—not in a whisper to an intimate friend, the doors and windows being previously closed, but in the public street! in a loud military voice!

assignments.text:
My next visit to Cranford was in the summer. There had been neither births,
deaths, nor marriages since I was there last. Everybody lived in the same
house, and wore pretty nearly the same well-preserved, old-fashioned clothes. The greatest event was, that Miss Jenkyns had purchased a new carpet for the
drawing-room. Oh, the busy work Miss Matty and I had in chasing the sunbeams,
as they fell in an afternoon right down on this carpet through the blindless
window!
assignments.summary: Mary returns to Cranford to find everything unchanged; the only notable event is Miss Jenkyns's purchase of a new carpet, which requires vigilant protection from sunlight.
assignments.best_quote: The greatest event was, that Miss Jenkyns had purchased a new carpet for the drawing-room. Oh, the busy work Miss Matty and I had in chasing the sunbeams, as they fell in an afternoon right down on this carpet through the blindless window!

assignments.text:
But to return to Miss Matty. It was really very pleasant to see how her
unselfishness and simple sense of justice called out the same good qualities in
others. She never seemed to think any one would impose upon her, because she
should be so grieved to do it to them.
assignments.summary: Miss Matty's kindness and trust inspire others to reciprocate her goodness; she never suspects dishonesty because she would never practise it.
assignments.best_quote: It was really very pleasant to see how her unselfishness and simple sense of justice called out the same good qualities in others.

assignments.text:
No! there was nothing she could teach to the rising generation of Cranford,
unless they had been quick learners and ready imitators of her patience, her
humility, her sweetness, her quiet contentment with all that she could not do.
I pondered and pondered until dinner was announced by Martha, with a face all
blubbered and swollen with crying.
assignments.summary: Mary concludes that Miss Matty has no teachable academic skills, but her true gifts—patience, humility, sweetness, and contentment—are virtues that cannot be commercialized.
assignments.best_quote: there was nothing she could teach to the rising generation of Cranford, unless they had been quick learners and ready imitators of her patience, her humility, her sweetness, her quiet contentment with all that she could not do

assignments.text:
He was a half-pay captain, and had obtained some situation on a
neighbouring railroad, which had been vehemently petitioned against by the
little town; and if, in addition to his masculine gender, and his connection
with the obnoxious railroad, he was so brazen as to talk of being
poor—why, then, indeed, he must be sent to Coventry. Death was as true
and as common as poverty; yet people never spoke about that, loud out in the
streets.
assignments.summary: Captain Brown's poverty confession is doubly offensive because he is a man connected to the disliked railway; poverty is a taboo subject like death.
assignments.best_quote: Death was as true and as common as poverty; yet people never spoke about that, loud out in the streets.

assignments.text:
All this
was borne by Miss Jessie and her father with more than placidity—with
absolute tenderness. I forgave Miss Jessie her singing out of tune, and her
juvenility of dress, when I saw her at home. I came to perceive that Captain
Brown’s dark Brutus wig and padded coat (alas! too often threadbare) were
remnants of the military smartness of his youth, which he now wore
unconsciously. He was a man of infinite resources, gained in his barrack
experience.
assignments.summary: Mary recognizes that the Browns' apparent affectations are actually the pathos of decline: the Captain's wig and coat are faded remnants of military life worn with unconscious dignity.
assignments.best_quote: I came to perceive that Captain Brown's dark Brutus wig and padded coat (alas! too often threadbare) were remnants of the military smartness of his youth, which he now wore unconsciously.

assignments.text:
Their dress is very independent of
fashion; as they observe, “What does it signify how we dress here at Cranford,
where everybody knows us?” And if they go from home, their reason is equally
cogent, “What does it signify how we dress here, where nobody knows us?” The
materials of their clothes are, in general, good and plain, and most of them
are nearly as scrupulous as Miss Tyler, of cleanly memory; but I will answer
for it, the last gigot, the last tight and scanty petticoat in wear in England,
was seen in Cranford—and seen without a smile.
assignments.summary: The Cranford ladies dress plainly and practically, indifferent to fashion; they maintain cleanliness but preserve old fashions without self-consciousness.
assignments.best_quote: What does it signify how we dress here at Cranford, where everybody knows us?

assignments.text:
She tried to speak quietly to me; but when she came to the actual fact that she
would have but about five shillings a week to live upon, she could not restrain
a few tears.
assignments.summary: Miss Matty attempts composure but breaks into tears when confronted with the reality of surviving on five shillings weekly.
assignments.best_quote: when she came to the actual fact that she would have but about five shillings a week to live upon, she could not restrain a few tears

assignments.text:
“I am not crying for myself, dear,” said she, wiping them away; “I believe I am
crying for the very silly thought of how my mother would grieve if she could
know; she always cared for us so much more than for herself. But many a poor
person has less, and I am not very extravagant, and, thank God, when the neck
of mutton, and Martha’s wages, and the rent are paid, I have not a farthing
owing. Poor Martha!
assignments.summary: Miss Matty clarifies that her tears are not for herself but for how her mother would grieve, and she expresses concern for her servant Martha.
assignments.best_quote: I am not crying for myself, dear. I believe I am crying for the very silly thought of how my mother would grieve if she could know; she always cared for us so much more than for herself

assignments.text:
I
thought of all the things by which a woman, past middle age, and with the
education common to ladies fifty years ago, could earn or add to a living
without materially losing caste; but at length I put even this last clause on
one side, and wondered what in the world Miss Matty could do.
assignments.summary: Mary considers what Miss Matty, as an older woman with education from fifty years ago, might do to earn money without losing caste, eventually abandoning even that concern.

assignments.text:
“Please, mum, it is true. I seed it myself,” and he shuddered at the
recollection. “The Captain was a-reading some new book as he was deep in,
a-waiting for the down train; and there was a little lass as wanted to come to
its mammy, and gave its sister the slip, and came toddling across the line.
assignments.summary: The carter explains that Captain Brown was absorbed in reading when he noticed a small child wandering onto the train tracks.
assignments.best_quote: The Captain was a-reading some new book as he was deep in, a-waiting for the down train; and there was a little lass as wanted to come to its mammy, and gave its sister the slip, and came toddling across the line.

assignments.text:
And
he looked up sudden, at the sound of the train coming, and seed the child, and
he darted on the line and cotched it up, and his foot slipped, and the train
came over him in no time. O Lord, Lord! Mum, it’s quite true, and they’ve come
over to tell his daughters. The child’s safe, though, with only a bang on its
shoulder as he threw it to its mammy.
assignments.summary: Captain Brown saved the child by throwing it to safety, but his foot slipped and the train killed him; the child was unharmed.
assignments.best_quote: And he looked up sudden, at the sound of the train coming, and seed the child, and he darted on the line and cotched it up, and his foot slipped, and the train came over him in no time.

assignments.text:
“Matilda, bring me my bonnet. I must go to those girls. God pardon me, if ever
I have spoken contemptuously to the Captain!”
assignments.summary: Miss Jenkyns immediately resolves to visit the grieving daughters and bitterly regrets any harsh words she has spoken to the Captain.
assignments.best_quote: Matilda, bring me my bonnet. I must go to those girls. God pardon me, if ever I have spoken contemptuously to the Captain!

assignments.text:
A light came into Miss Jessie’s face. “Would it comfort you, dearest, to think
that he does know?—would it comfort you, love, to know that his cares,
his sorrows”—Her voice quivered, but she steadied it into
calmness—“Mary! he has gone before you to the place where the weary are
at rest. He knows now how you loved him.”
assignments.summary: Miss Jessie gently tells her sister that their father is already dead and in heaven, where he now knows how much she loved him.
assignments.best_quote: Would it comfort you, dearest, to think that he does know?—would it comfort you, love, to know that his cares, his sorrows—Her voice quivered, but she steadied it into calmness—Mary! he has gone before you to the place where the weary are at rest. He knows now how you loved him.

assignments.text:
The next day a
full account of the fatal accident was in the county paper which Miss Jenkyns
took in. Her eyes were very weak, she said, and she asked me to read it. When I
came to the “gallant gentleman was deeply engaged in the perusal of a number of
‘Pickwick,’ which he had just received,” Miss Jenkyns shook her head long and
solemnly, and then sighed out, “Poor, dear, infatuated man!”
assignments.summary: The newspaper account notes that Captain Brown was reading a number of Pickwick when the accident occurred; Miss Jenkyns sighs with long regret.
assignments.best_quote: Poor, dear, infatuated man!

assignments.text:
She read one of the conversations between Rasselas and Imlac, in a
high-pitched, majestic voice: and when she had ended, she said, “I imagine I am
now justified in my preference of Dr Johnson as a writer of fiction.” The
Captain screwed his lips up, and drummed on the table, but he did not speak.
She thought she would give him a finishing blow or two.
assignments.summary: Miss Jenkyns reads the Rasselas conversation in majestic tones and declares Johnson superior to Dickens; the Captain screws up his lips in frustration.
assignments.best_quote: I imagine I am now justified in my preference of Dr Johnson as a writer of fiction

assignments.text:
Perhaps they entertained him with ‘the feast of reason
and the flow of soul’; and to us, who are acquainted with Captain Brown’s sad
want of relish for ‘the pure wells of English undefiled,’ it may be matter for
congratulation that he has had the opportunity of improving his taste by
holding converse with an elegant and refined member of the British aristocracy. But from some mundane failings who is altogether free?”
assignments.summary: Miss Jenkyns sarcastically suggests that the Captain's lowbrow literary taste (favoring Boz) may have been improved by conversing with the refined aristocrat, while making a philosophical comment on human weakness.
assignments.best_quote: Perhaps they entertained him with 'the feast of reason and the flow of soul'; and to us, who are acquainted with Captain Brown's sad want of relish for 'the pure wells of English undefiled,' it may be matter for congratulation that he has had the opportunity of improving his taste by holding converse with an elegant and refined member of the British aristocracy. But from some mundane failings who is altogether free?

assignments.text:
Captain Brown and Miss Jenkyns were not very cordial to each other. The
literary dispute, of which I had seen the beginning, was a “raw,” the slightest
touch on which made them wince. It was the only difference of opinion they had
ever had; but that difference was enough.
assignments.summary: The argument between Captain Brown and Miss Jenkyns over Dr Johnson versus Mr Boz remains an open wound between them.
assignments.best_quote: The literary dispute, of which I had seen the beginning, was a "raw," the slightest touch on which made them wince.

assignments.text:
Old gowns, white and
venerable collars, any number of brooches, up and down and everywhere (some
with dogs’ eyes painted in them; some that were like small picture-frames with
mausoleums and weeping-willows neatly executed in hair inside; some, again,
with miniatures of ladies and gentlemen sweetly smiling out of a nest of stiff
muslin), old brooches for a permanent ornament, and new caps to suit the
fashion of the day—the ladies of Cranford always dressed with chaste
elegance and propriety, as Miss Barker once prettily expressed it.
assignments.summary: The narrator provides an affectionate, detailed inventory of the Cranford ladies' decorative brooches—featuring painted dog eyes, hair mausoleums with weeping willows, and miniature portraits—alongside their conservative dress, capturing their sentimental gentility.
assignments.best_quote: Old gowns, white and venerable collars, any number of brooches, up and down and everywhere (some with dogs' eyes painted in them; some that were like small picture-frames with mausoleums and weeping-willows neatly executed in hair inside; some, again, with miniatures of ladies and gentlemen sweetly smiling out of a nest of stiff muslin), old brooches for a permanent ornament, and new caps to suit the fashion of the day—the ladies of Cranford always dressed with chaste elegance and propriety, as Miss Barker once prettily expressed it.

assignments.text:
In spite of the uncomfortable feeling which this last consideration gave me, I
could not help being amused at Jenny’s position, which was exceedingly like
that of a witness being examined and cross-examined by two counsel who are not
at all scrupulous about asking leading questions. The conclusion I arrived at
was, that Jenny had certainly seen something beyond what a fit of indigestion
would have caused.
assignments.summary: Mary notes Jenny's position resembles a witness examined and cross-examined by rival lawyers; Mary concludes Jenny has seen something real, beyond indigestion alone.

assignments.text:
I cannot abide the wine now, nor the scent of the
flowers; they turn me sick and faint, as they did that day, when Peter came in,
looking as haughty as any man—indeed, looking like a man, not like a boy. ‘Mother!’ he said, ‘I am come to say, God bless you for ever.’ I saw his lips
quiver as he spoke; and I think he durst not say anything more loving, for the
purpose that was in his heart.
assignments.summary: Peter enters the store-room where his mother works, gives her a formal blessing, then embraces her intensely; his quivering lips and hidden resolve suggest he is saying goodbye forever.
assignments.best_quote: 'Mother!' he said, 'I am come to say, God bless you for ever.' I saw his lips quiver as he spoke; and I think he durst not say anything more loving, for the purpose that was in his heart.

assignments.text:
“He had made his way to Liverpool; and there was war then; and some of the
king’s ships lay off the mouth of the Mersey; and they were only too glad to
have a fine likely boy such as him (five foot nine he was), come to offer
himself. The captain wrote to my father, and Peter wrote to my mother. Stay!
those letters will be somewhere here.”
assignments.summary: Peter fled to Liverpool and voluntarily enlisted in the Navy during wartime; the ship's captain eventually wrote to Peter's father.
assignments.best_quote: He had made his way to Liverpool; and there was war then; and some of the king's ships lay off the mouth of the Mersey; and they were only too glad to have a fine likely boy such as him (five foot nine he was), come to offer himself.

assignments.text:
“Yes, once. He came home a lieutenant; he did not get to be admiral. And he and
my father were such friends! My father took him into every house in the parish,
he was so proud of him. He never walked out without Peter’s arm to lean upon. Deborah used to smile (I don’t think we ever laughed again after my mother’s
death), and say she was quite put in a corner.
assignments.summary: Peter returns as a naval lieutenant; the father receives him with joy and pride, walking arm-in-arm with his son everywhere in the parish.
assignments.best_quote: 'Yes, once. He came home a lieutenant; he did not get to be admiral. And he and my father were such friends! My father took him into every house in the parish, he was so proud of him. He never walked out without Peter's arm to lean upon.'

assignments.text:
“Then Peter went to sea again; and, by-and-by, my father died, blessing us
both, and thanking Deborah for all she had been to him; and, of course, our
circumstances were changed; and, instead of living at the rectory, and keeping
three maids and a man, we had to come to this small house, and be content with
a servant-of-all-work; but, as Deborah used to say, we have always lived
genteelly, even if circumstances have compelled us to simplicity. Poor
Deborah!”
assignments.summary: Peter returns to the Navy; their father dies, blessing both daughters and especially thanking Deborah; the family's fortunes decline, they leave the rectory for a small house, but maintain their gentility.
assignments.best_quote: 'Then Peter went to sea again; and, by-and-by, my father died, blessing us both, and thanking Deborah for all she had been to him; and, of course, our circumstances were changed; and, instead of living at the rectory, and keeping three maids and a man, we had to come to this small house, and be content with a servant-of-all-work; but, as Deborah used to say, we have always lived genteelly, even if circumstances have compelled us to simplicity.'

assignments.text:
But now that the days were longer
and more cheerful, he was beginning to urge the necessity of my return; and I
only delayed in a sort of odd forlorn hope that if I could obtain any clear
information, I might make the account given by the signora of the Aga Jenkyns
tally with that of “poor Peter,” his appearance and disappearance, which I had
winnowed out of the conversation of Miss Pole and Mrs Forrester.
assignments.summary: Mary delays her return home hoping to verify whether the Signora's account of the Aga matches the information she has gathered about poor Peter.

assignments.text:
With my idea of the rector derived from a
picture in the dining-parlour, stiff and stately, in a huge full-bottomed wig,
with gown, cassock, and bands, and his hand upon a copy of the only sermon he
ever published—it was strange to read these letters. They were full of
eager, passionate ardour; short homely sentences, right fresh from the heart
(very different from the grand Latinised, Johnsonian style of the printed
sermon preached before some judge at assize time).
assignments.summary: Mary notes the portrait of the rector shows him stiff and formal in full ecclesiastical dress, contrasting sharply with his passionate, ardent love-letters.
assignments.best_quote: stiff and stately, in a huge full-bottomed wig, with gown, cassock, and bands... it was strange to read these letters. They were full of eager, passionate ardour; short homely sentences, right fresh from the heart

assignments.text:
I saw the tears
stealing down the well-worn furrows of Miss Matty’s cheeks, and her spectacles
often wanted wiping. I trusted at last that she would light the other candle,
for my own eyes were rather dim, and I wanted more light to see the pale, faded
ink; but no, even through her tears, she saw and remembered her little
economical ways.
assignments.summary: Miss Matty weeps while reading the letters; despite her tears, she refuses to light a second candle, maintaining her economy.
assignments.best_quote: even through her tears, she saw and remembered her little economical ways

assignments.text:
I had once said, on receiving a present of an elaborate pair,
that I should feel quite tempted to drop one of them in the street, in order to
have it admired; but I found this little joke (and it was a very little one)
was such a distress to her sense of propriety, and was taken with such anxious,
earnest alarm, lest the temptation might some day prove too strong for me, that
I quite regretted having ventured upon it.
assignments.summary: Mary joked about wanting to drop a garter in the street to have it admired, but this caused Miss Matty genuine anxiety about temptation to impropriety.
assignments.best_quote: I should feel quite tempted to drop one of them in the street, in order to have it admired

assignments.text:
Jenny came back with a white face of terror. “Oh, ma’am! Oh, Miss Jenkyns,
ma’am! Captain Brown is killed by them nasty cruel railroads!” and she burst
into tears. She, along with many others, had experienced the poor Captain’s
kindness.
assignments.summary: Jenny tearfully announces that Captain Brown has been killed by the railroad, having experienced his kindness as many have.
assignments.best_quote: Captain Brown is killed by them nasty cruel railroads!

assignments.text:
I don’t think I ever dream of any words or sound she makes; she is very
noiseless and still, but she comes to me when she is very sorry or very glad,
and I have wakened with the clasp of her dear little arms round my neck.
assignments.summary: Miss Matty describes her dream child as silent but responsive, coming to her in moments of sorrow and joy, with tactile presence that haunts her waking.
assignments.best_quote: she comes to me when she is very sorry or very glad, and I have wakened with the clasp of her dear little arms round my neck

assignments.text:
“My dear, that boy’s trick, on that sunny day, when all seemed going straight
and well, broke my mother’s heart, and changed my father for life. It did,
indeed. Old Clare said, Peter looked as white as my father; and stood as still
as a statue to be flogged; and my father struck hard! When my father stopped to
take breath, Peter said, ‘Have you done enough, sir?’ quite hoarsely, and still
standing quite quiet.
assignments.summary: Peter bears the flogging in stoic silence; old Clare witnesses his white face and unflinching posture, and reveals that this shocking public incident broke the mother's heart and permanently changed the father.
assignments.best_quote: 'Have you done enough, sir?' quite hoarsely, and still standing quite quiet.

assignments.text:
It was warm May weather, so only the
little half-door was closed; and Miss Matty sat behind the counter, knitting an
elaborate pair of garters; elaborate they seemed to me, but the difficult
stitch was no weight upon her mind, for she was singing in a low voice to
herself as her needles went rapidly in and out.
assignments.summary: Miss Matty sits behind her counter in warm May weather, knitting elaborate garters while contentedly humming to herself.
assignments.best_quote: she was singing in a low voice to herself as her needles went rapidly in and out

assignments.text:
He had been travelling in the East, and was on his return home when, at Rome,
he saw the account of Captain Brown’s death in  Galignani .
assignments.summary: Major Gordon was traveling in the East and saw Captain Brown's death reported in an Italian newspaper, prompting his return to England.
